questions.prompt: Where does each item belong? Pick the one place that fits best.
questions.explain: The instructions file holds stable rules you write. Auto memory holds notes the tool wrote itself. A handoff note holds the state of one task (what failed, what is next). Git history holds the commits and their messages.

items.misconception: A standing rule that applies to every session belongs in the instructions file, which loads every session; a handoff note covers one task.

items.text: Prefers sample_id over id as the column name: a line you never typed, found listed by /memory after two corrections
items.misconception: You did not write it and the harness decided to keep it, which is what makes it auto memory.

items.text: Tried a trim at Q15, it dropped 40% of reads, do not retry
items.misconception: This is the state of one task and tells the next session what not to repeat. A standing rule would apply to all work.

items.text: a1b2c3d qc: vectorise the mean-quality calculation
items.misconception: A commit message is stored with the commit, in the repository history, so it does not belong in a notes file.

items.text: Next step: rerun the filter on batch 2 with the new threshold
items.misconception: A next step is only true until it is done. A stable instructions file would soon be wrong if it held it.

questions.prompt: Lines from a handoff note written at the end of a session in which only sample_A was compared with the old output. Which line overstates what was verified?
questions.explain: A claim of verification must say what was run and on what. This line claims every sample matched but names no command and no sample, and only sample_A was compared. The next session would trust it and skip the check.

lines.text: Goal: replace the per-read loop in qc_filter.py with a vectorised version
lines.why: A plain statement of intent that makes no claim about results.

lines.text: Verified: matches old output on all samples
Not verified: behaviour on reads shorter than 30 bases
lines.why: It says openly what was not checked.

lines.text: Decision: keep the old function mean_qual() until all samples are compared
lines.why: It records a decision and the condition for dropping it.

questions.prompt: The agent drafted your handoff note and wrote: 'All tests pass.' You did not see it run them. What do you do before giving the note to a fresh session?
questions.explain: A drafted note can overstate what was checked. Run the tests yourself, or edit the line to say what was actually run. Then the next session starts from a true statement.

options.text: Run the tests, then fix the line to match the result
Keep it, since the agent wrote it with the whole session in view
options.misconception: Having seen the session is different from having checked it; models can state more certainty than the work supports.

options.text: Delete the note and let auto memory carry the state
options.misconception: Auto memory holds what the tool chose to save, so it may hold nothing about this task's state.

options.text: Ask the agent in the same session if it is sure
options.misconception: A confident yes comes from the same writer, so a check needs a command or a test.

questions.prompt: A fresh session starts with your handoff note in the repo. Which first prompt gives you a check on its understanding?
questions.explain: Asking for a restatement before any change lets you compare it with the real state: a cheap comprehension check that works best alongside your own look at the real state, since the same model wrote the restatement. Starting work at once can hide a misunderstanding inside new edits.

options.text: Read HANDOFF.md and tell me what you understand before editing
Read HANDOFF.md and then carry out the listed next steps in order
options.misconception: If the note is misread, the error shows up only as wrong edits you must then find and undo; a restatement first catches it more cheaply.
A fresh session has no history, so the agent has nothing to continue from and may invent it.

options.text: Summarise what you remember of yesterday's session with me
options.misconception: A fresh session has no copy of yesterday's session, so it can only guess.

questions.prompt: Match each risk to the habit that counters it.
questions.explain: Each habit answers one risk: check what a draft claims, verify what the tool wrote itself, and compare a restatement with the real state before any edit.

pairs.left: The agent's draft note says 'all tests pass' but you never saw them run
pairs.right: Run them yourself, or edit the line to say what was actually run
pairs.misconception: Keeping the line because the agent wrote it passes an unchecked claim to the next session.

pairs.left: Auto memory holds a wrong column name that loads every session
pairs.right: Read it with /memory and verify it before trusting it
pairs.misconception: Memory is loaded as written; nothing checks it for you.

pairs.left: A fresh session may have misread the handoff note
pairs.right: Ask for its restatement before any edits and compare it with the real state
pairs.misconception: Letting it start work at once hides a misreading inside new edits.
